ladder.analysis: This term continues a structural shift in how the Supreme Court operates: emergency ('shadow docket') rulings, which are fast, largely unexplained, and skip full briefing or oral argument, now outnumber traditional merits decisions reached after months of litigation. That shift matters because lower-court judges say they lack guidance from these abbreviated rulings, and the Trump administration has increasingly used emergency appeals to bypass lower courts it views as unfavorable. Separately, the Court's docket reflects a broader doctrinal move on religion—away from strict church-state separation toward expanded free-exercise protections—raising the possibility that taxpayer funding could be extended to religious schools that maintain discriminatory admissions policies. Other cases, on guns, climate liability, and immigration detention and deportation policy, extend ongoing legal disputes over the scope of state regulatory power versus individual and corporate rights, and over executive authority in immigration enforcement.
ladder.steelman: Lower court judges across the ideological spectrum—both liberal and conservative—have complained that the Supreme Court's brief, often unexplained emergency-docket rulings fail to give them adequate guidance, even as such rulings now outnumber the Court's full merits decisions.
ladder.implications: The outcomes in the religion, gun, and immigration cases could reset decades-old precedents on church-state separation, state firearm regulation, and executive deportation authority, while the growing reliance on the emergency docket means future high-stakes rulings—on elections or other urgent disputes—may arrive with less public explanation and less advance notice than traditional merits decisions.

stories.headline: Trump creates 'Super Intelligence Force' led by DNI Jay Clayton to ensure US AI dominance

claims.text: On Sunday, President Trump announced via a Truth Social post the creation of a new federal body called the 'Super Intelligence Force' (SIF).
Trump named Jay Clayton, the current Director of National Intelligence, to lead the SIF and serve as the White House's new AI czar.
Clayton previously served as the top federal prosecutor in Manhattan and led the Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump's first term.

According to Trump's post, the SIF is tasked with coordinating the federal government's engagement with consumers, public-interest groups, religious organizations, critical infrastructure providers, and AI companies.
CBS News was the first outlet to report Clayton's appointment as AI czar.
In September, Trump had already announced plans for an 'AI Force' and a czar role to oversee AI growth, and he floated Clayton's name for the position at that time.

David Sacks previously served as the administration's AI and cryptocurrency czar until March 2026, when he reached his employment limit as a 'special government employee'; he continues to co-chair the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology.
On the Tuesday before the SIF announcement, Trump and six AI industry executives signed an AI accord at the White House creating internal and external monitors meant to address AI safety issues.

The announcement formalizes an AI-oversight structure that Trump first previewed in September, consolidating it under Jay Clayton, who already runs the nation's 18 intelligence agencies as Director of National Intelligence.
The move follows warnings from AI researchers that the technology is advancing faster than safeguards can keep pace.
The announcement comes amid the administration's broader push to maintain U.S. leadership over China in AI development.

The SIF appears designed to serve a dual function: advancing the administration's stated goal of global AI dominance while also managing public and industry-facing coordination on safety-related concerns.
The AI accord signed with tech executives just days before the SIF was unveiled underscores a balance between AI dominance and safety coordination.
The appointment places both the nation's top intelligence official and its lead AI-policy coordinator in the hands of one person.

stories.headline: Federal judge rules Congress cannot bar noncitizens from voting in federal elections

claims.text: U.S. District Judge David Leibowitz of the Southern District of Florida issued a 31-page ruling on Thursday dismissing federal charges against Chelsea Cox.
Chelsea Cox is a woman from Jamaica accused of voting in federal elections from 2012 to 2020 while not a U.S. citizen.
Cox allegedly overstayed a tourist visa by 20 years.
Cox allegedly used a fraudulent U.S. Virgin Islands birth certificate to obtain a Florida driver's license.
Cox allegedly used that Florida driver's license to register to vote.
The case centered on 18 U.S.C. § 611, the 'Voting by Aliens' law, enacted in 1996 as part of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act (IIRIRA).
18 U.S.C. § 611 prohibits noncitizens from voting in federal elections.
Leibowitz ruled the statute unconstitutional as applied to Cox.
Leibowitz held that the Constitution gives states — not Congress — the authority to set voter qualifications in federal elections.
Leibowitz appointed Paul D. Clement, a former U.S. Solicitor General, as amicus curiae.
Clement and co-counsel Chadwick J. Harper argued the law's 'unless' clause showed Congress's intent to override state voting permissions.
Judge Leibowitz was nominated by President Biden in 2024.
Judge Leibowitz was confirmed by the Senate 64-33.
Then-Sen. Marco Rubio, R-Fla., voted in favor of confirming Judge Leibowitz.
Florida retains the authority to bring separate state charges against Cox despite the dismissal of federal charges.
According to a Reuters investigation cited by Jurist, Cox was one of only 129 people charged under the federal noncitizen-voting law.
According to that Reuters investigation, no defendants were accused of conspiring to sway an election, back a candidate, or accept payment for a vote.

The ruling addresses a previously untested constitutional question: whether Congress had authority under the Constitution to criminalize noncitizen voting in federal elections, or whether that power belongs exclusively to the states under the Constitution's voter-qualification framework.

Judge Leibowitz concluded that while Congress holds broad power over immigration and naturalization, that power does not extend to overriding the states' express constitutional authority to set voter qualifications.
Judge Leibowitz concluded that the statute in question created a federal voter qualification rather than regulating election procedures or fraud.
The decision arrives amid a broader national push by the Trump administration to restrict and prosecute noncitizen voting.
The Trump administration's push includes efforts to verify citizenship on state voter rolls.
The decision arrives amid a stalled Senate push for the SAVE Act, which would impose federal citizenship-verification requirements for voter registration.

Legal experts cited in the coverage noted competing precedents — including Bluman v. FEC (addressing foreign nationals' campaign spending, not voting prosecutions) and Oregon v. Mitchell (addressing federal authority over voting age) — that could factor into an appeal to the 11th Circuit Court of Appeals.

The dispute reflects a genuine, unresolved constitutional tension between two textual provisions — the states' explicit authority to set voter qualifications and Congress's broad naturalization power.
Legal experts across the spectrum expect the ruling to be closely scrutinized on appeal.
Legal experts cited in the coverage have suggested the ruling is likely to be challenged on appeal.
Some legal experts predict the ruling could be overturned given competing precedents on federal versus state authority over voter qualifications in federal elections.

stories.headline: Brazil votes in polarised presidential election between Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro
body: Brazilians began voting on Sunday in a general election that pits left-wing incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva against right-wing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of convicted former President Jair Bolsonaro. About 160 million registered voters are eligible to cast ballots in the election, which also chooses lawmakers, governors and senators. If no presidential candidate wins more than 50 percent of valid votes, the top two contenders will proceed to a run-off on October 25.

Opinion polls show a close race, with Lula and Bolsonaro both hovering around the 40 percent mark and Lula holding a marginal advantage. The other 11 candidates are polling at 4 percent or less. With about 9 percent of voters still undecided or planning to spoil their ballot, an outright first-round win cannot be entirely ruled out, though a run-off is considered highly likely. Voting is compulsory for literate Brazilians aged 18 to 70, with a fine for those who do not cast a ballot.

Lula, 80, of the Workers’ Party, is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term. He previously served as president from 2003 to 2010, lifting millions out of poverty through the Bolsa Família cash-transfer program. He left office with record approval ratings but was later convicted of corruption and money laundering, charges he denied; those convictions were annulled in 2021, allowing him to win the 2022 election against Jair Bolsonaro by 1.8 percentage points. During his current term, Lula has pointed to reduced deforestation in the Amazon as a policy success, but has drawn criticism from environmentalists for supporting exploratory oil drilling near the Amazon river mouth. He has also had rocky relations with US President Donald Trump, insisting that “Brazil does not fit into anyone’s backyard.”

Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, of the Liberal Party, is appealing to supporters of his father by promising to continue his tough-on-crime and pro-gun policies, and to cut regulations on farmers. He has courted evangelicals and the agricultural industry, and has actively sought alliance with the Trump administration, promising to join the US-led anti-crime alliance “Shield of the Americas” if elected. After voting in Rio de Janeiro on Sunday, Bolsonaro said he wants to “free the Brazilian people” and that “Brazil needs change … it cannot bear any more suffering, such as high taxes, so many women killed.” He expressed confidence in a first-round victory.

The election is deeply shaped by the shadow of Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election and is barred from office. Under house arrest due to health problems, he is prohibited from posting on social media or making public statements, but an AI-generated avatar of him endorsed his son’s campaign. A scandal involving jailed banker Daniel Vorcaro, accused of orchestrating a major financial fraud, has pushed corruption to the top of voters’ concerns. Flávio Bolsonaro faces a police investigation for suspected corruption and money laundering over Vorcaro’s alleged financing of a biopic about his father. Alleged links between Vorcaro and Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who presided over Jair Bolsonaro’s trial, have also emerged; Moraes has denied wrongdoing. Lula has said “no one is above the law,” while Bolsonaro has told supporters, “Voting for Lula means voting for Moraes.”

stories.headline: Russia strikes Kyiv bridge for second day as German chancellor Merz visits Ukraine
stories.byline: International & World desk · anchored on Reuters
body: A Russian drone struck the Pivnichnyi (Northern) Bridge in Kyiv for the second consecutive day on Sunday, injuring two people, as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz made an unannounced visit to the Ukrainian capital in a show of support. The attack came as Moscow intensified strikes on critical infrastructure, hitting a second major bridge across the Dnipro River that links the city's eastern and western halves.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the strike damaged the roadway and overhead trolleybus wires, causing traffic jams. Video verified by the BBC shows a drone crashing into the bridge and exploding, leaving a gaping hole in a traffic lane. The Pivdennyi (Southern) Bridge was hit multiple times earlier in the week. A separate drone strike damaged a heating main, temporarily cutting hot water in the north-eastern Desnyanskyi district. Ukraine's Air Force reported that Russia launched 135 drones overnight, of which 125 were shot down. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a warehouse in Sumy was struck, killing one person, and a communications facility in Dnipro was hit, injuring six.

Merz met Zelenskyy and laid wreaths for fallen Ukrainian soldiers. Writing on X, Merz said: "Ukraine is facing decisive weeks. That is why I travelled to Kyiv today with the message: You can rely on us." A new aid package worth more than €1.3bn ($1.5bn) was agreed, including weapons and support for Ukraine's energy sector ahead of winter. Al Jazeera reported the package includes $1.1bn in military aid and $394m for energy repairs. Merz was accompanied by his economy minister and executives from Siemens Energy and Diehl Defence. The pair visited the National Academy of Sciences, damaged by a Russian drone on September 28, as air raid sirens sounded across the city.

Russia's defence ministry said it would intensify strikes across Ukraine in response to Zelenskyy's comments about ramping up attacks on Russian oil refineries. Moscow repeated a warning for foreign citizens, including diplomats, to leave Kyiv. EU ambassador Katarína Mathernová responded on X: "The EU Delegation is staying. Threatening us will not stop Europe's support for Ukraine." German ambassador Boris Ruge added: "Amen - we're staying." Russian President Vladimir Putin said his military was carrying out retaliatory attacks following Ukraine's strikes on Russian energy facilities, despite Moscow having launched such attacks first. Russia currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.

The two bridges are still standing, but damage and traffic restrictions have caused gridlock. About 500,000 vehicles use the bridges daily. Kyiv resident Roman told the BBC: "To get from the left bank to the right one and back - it's just hell." Officials are planning temporary pontoon bridges, ferry services, and a tunnel under the river. Klitschko warned the city is in a "very dramatic situation" as Moscow batters "critical infrastructure, logistics, housing" and other key facilities. Experts say repeated drone attacks are unlikely to bring down the bridges but could force their closure and weaken their structure.

Since becoming chancellor in May 2025, Merz has made Germany the single largest donor to Ukraine. He said the country "needs all our support in the coming weeks", adding: "If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us." The visit underscores Western backing as the war enters its fifth year, with both sides increasing drone and missile strikes on infrastructure and military sites.

stories.headline: Iran says Strait of Hormuz will remain closed until US meets conditions
stories.byline: International & World desk · anchored on Reuters
body: Iran’s parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said on Sunday that the Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until the United States meets seven conditions based on the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, according to the state-linked news agency Nournews. Ghalibaf stated that Washington had recently put forward proposals through a mediator, but warned that “the era of wasting time and dictating unilateral demands is over.” He added that Iran is “present on the military battlefield and will confront them with new surprises.”

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi separately said that a plan put forward by Tehran could lead to the route reopening within seven days if accepted. Speaking to foreign ambassadors in Tehran, Araghchi said Iran is “serious about finding diplomatic solutions just as we are serious about defending ourselves.” He warned that if the US takes military action again, Iran is “more prepared than before and will take whatever action is necessary to defend ourselves.”

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said that reopening the strait has been Tehran’s main goal, while the US has continued to focus on nuclear talks. The Strait of Hormuz has been largely blocked and disrupted for more than seven months since the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran on February 28, causing one of the worst maritime shipping disruptions in decades. The waterway normally handles about one-fifth of global oil and natural gas shipments.

US President Donald Trump ruled out an Iranian proposal to reopen the strait last week. On Sunday, Trump told reporters that an imminent decision will be made on Iran, warning that the only question is whether Tehran will have it the “easy way or hard way.” He claimed that Iran has been “decimated” and has “virtually given up any plans for a nuclear weapon.”

Separately, Yemen’s Houthi rebels claimed responsibility for a ballistic missile attack on a Saudi Aramco oil refinery in Riyadh, saying it was retaliation for Saudi coalition airstrikes on Sanaa and other Yemeni provinces. Witnesses reported seeing a large plume of smoke and fire near an Aramco installation in the capital. Yemeni government-aligned forces said they conducted 97 “precision targeting operations” against the Houthis, neutralizing 260 militia members, according to military spokesperson Brigadier General Majid Abdullah Al-Nuzaili.

stories.headline: Ukrainian Robot Offensive Recaptures Territory; Russian Drones Violate Moldova and Strike Kyiv Bridges
stories.byline: International & World desk · anchored on Reuters
body: Ukrainian forces have recaptured 176 square kilometers of territory in the Donbas region through a surprise robot offensive, dubbed Operation Vivaldi, which began in May, according to reports from CNBC and security experts. The operation, conducted by Ukraine’s Third Army Corps, has inflicted over 2,000 Russian casualties and taken more than 250 Russian soldiers prisoner, Ukrainian Brigadier-General Andrii Biletskyi said on September 28. Meanwhile, Russian forces escalated long-range strikes, hitting Kyiv’s Northern Bridge on October 3 and sending five drones, including Banderol loitering munitions, into Moldovan airspace, where they crashed, according to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW).

Operation Vivaldi involved the deployment of large bomber drones and remote-controlled robots behind Russian lines around Lyman in northern Donetsk Oblast, catching Russian forces off guard, security experts told CNBC. Patrick Bolder, a defense expert at the Hague Center for Strategic Studies, described the offensive as a "big bloody nose" to Russia’s minimal war aim of seizing the Donbas. Ukrainian forces secured control of the air in the area, denying Russia use of its drones, then used their own drones to drop unmanned ground vehicles behind enemy lines. "They put this together masterly," Bolder said. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy lauded the operation, stating that replacing warriors with ground robotic systems wherever possible is "one particularly promising area" and that Ukraine will scale up the use of drones for the most dangerous tasks.

Russian drone incursions into Moldova have become increasingly frequent, with five drones—including Banderol loitering munitions—violating Moldovan airspace on October 3, the Moldovan government reported. Debris fell in the Causeni, Hincesti, Anenii Noi, and Stefan Voda districts and near Crocmaz. ISW assessed that the violation, involving more aerial vehicles than previous incidents, is part of Moscow’s efforts to normalize airspace violations with increasingly intense and frequent incursions. Since August alone, seven violations have been recorded.

Russian forces struck the Northern Bridge over the Dnipro River in Kyiv City on October 3, the sixth strike on bridges since October 1, Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko reported. ISW noted that Russian forces have targeted both the Southern and Northern bridges to degrade transportation and logistics across the Dnipro River, aiming to split Kyiv physically and make life difficult for civilians to force Ukraine to capitulate. The Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs issued a warning on October 3, recommending foreign citizens and diplomats leave Kyiv and stating that Russian forces will continue long-range strikes. Ukrainian Presidential Advisor on Defense Technologies Serhiy “Flash” Beskrestnov reported that Russian forces used mesh network repeaters to maintain control of drone trajectories during strikes on the bridges.

Ukraine continued its own long-range strike campaign against Russian missile and drone launch sites, President Zelenskyy stated on October 3, reporting a strike on an Iskander ballistic missile launch system in Bryansk Oblast. Ukraine’s Strategic Communications Center added that forces struck a Russian strike drone launch complex near Tsimbulova, Oryol Oblast on the night of October 2–3. Russia launched 157 drones against Ukraine overnight and Banderol loitering munitions on the morning of October 3, according to ISW.

The developments underscore the evolving nature of the conflict, with Ukraine seeking to raise the cost of Russia’s war by targeting oil refineries and logistics hubs, as noted by CNBC. Security experts cautioned that Ukraine’s robot offensive, while significant, is not a decisive breakthrough but sends "a powerful message to Moscow and to Kyiv’s partners that the highly innovative Ukrainian military remains capable of defeating Russia on the battlefield," said David Kirichenko of the Henry Jackson Society. Serhii Kuzan, chairman of the Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Center, said Operation Vivaldi "demonstrated that the systematic replacement of human personnel with robots is changing the paradigm of modern warfare."

stories.headline: Ethiopian government forces seize Tigray capital Mekelle as TPLF withdraws
body: Ethiopian government forces and allied fighters have taken control of Mekelle, the capital of the northern Tigray region, after the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) announced it had temporarily withdrawn from the city. The TPLF said in a statement late Saturday that it had 'temporarily moved out of Mekelle' to 'operate from somewhere else,' citing concerns about risks to civilians. Two residents told the BBC that pro-government forces now control the city and that TPLF forces have abandoned it; one resident said mobile phone services appeared to have resumed in parts of Mekelle. A humanitarian source and a Mekelle resident confirmed to Reuters that the city was under government control, and a humanitarian source told AFP that staff on the ground reported the TPLF had abandoned the regional capital, with Ethiopian federal forces and allied forces observed across various locations.

The recapture of Mekelle's main airport by Ethiopia's federal army and pro-government fighters preceded the TPLF's withdrawal. The development marks a major shift in the conflict, which erupted on September 23 after seven armed and political groups—including the TPLF and the Fano militia from Amhara—announced an alliance aimed at removing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government and establishing an inclusive transitional administration. The fighting has spread across parts of Ethiopia's northern regions of Tigray, Afar and Amhara.

The renewed hostilities follow the collapse of a 2022 peace deal, known as the Pretoria Agreement, brokered by the African Union that ended a devastating two-year civil war between the federal government and Tigray forces. The AU's mediator estimated some 600,000 people died in that conflict, which drove the region to the precipice of famine. In the last six months, relations have worsened, with both sides accusing each other of violating the agreement.

The latest round of violence has raised fears of a wider war that could draw in neighbouring countries. Ethiopia has accused Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt of backing the opposition coalition; Khartoum and Cairo have denied involvement. On Friday, Ethiopia and Eritrea severed diplomatic relations after Addis Ababa accused Asmara of supporting the new rebel alliance, a charge Eritrea denied. Ethiopia also expelled an Egyptian diplomat, prompting Cairo to order an Ethiopian embassy official to leave within the same period.

The United States has urged Ethiopia and Eritrea 'to respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of their neighbors, exercise maximum restraint and return to dialogue and cooperation,' warning that the increasing tensions 'have the potential to affect the entire region.' The US Department of State called for 'restraint' and 'dialogue' on all sides ahead of a diplomatic meeting in Egypt on Sunday with leaders from some of Ethiopia's neighbours. Egypt's President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, addressing the African Union's mid-year coordination summit in El-Alamein, said Egypt opposed foreign interference in African states and called for relations based on 'mutual respect, good neighbourliness, dialogue and consultation.' The United Nations has warned that the deteriorating security situation in northern Ethiopia is severely disrupting humanitarian work and has called on all sides to guarantee safe and unhindered access to people in need.

stories.headline: Q3 Earnings Season Opens With Record Corporate Optimism; Early Results Beat Estimates
body: The third-quarter earnings season kicked off this week with a record level of corporate optimism about future profits, according to MarketWatch. More companies than ever have expressed upbeat outlooks for their bottom lines as reporting begins.

Early results from the S&P 500 have been strong. According to Seeking Alpha’s Earnings Scoreboard, all eight S&P 500 firms that reported so far beat earnings-per-share estimates, and six of those saw year-over-year profit increases. The scoreboard includes companies such as Nike, Micron Technology, Carnival, Accenture, Conagra Brands, McCormick & Company, Jabil, FactSet, PepsiCo, Delta Air Lines, and Constellation Brands.

The first full week of October, while light on reports, features a diverse earnings slate spanning consumer staples, beverages, travel, apparel, and AI infrastructure, according to Seeking Alpha. Companies reporting include PepsiCo, Delta Air Lines, Constellation Brands, Tilray Brands, Levi Strauss & Co., and others. These results are expected to offer fresh reads on consumer demand and the capital-intensive technology buildout.

Investors are preparing for the earnings season as major names like Delta and Pepsi report this week, Investopedia noted. Forbes highlighted that the S&P 500 Q3 earnings preview points to key trends investors need to watch, though specific details on those trends were not provided in the available material.

stories.headline: Investors brace for potential stock market correction amid mixed signals
body: Investors are confronting the possibility of a stock market correction as a confluence of warning signs — from elevated valuations to rising bond yields — echoes conditions that preceded previous downturns. Since 1945, the U.S. stock market has endured 37 corrections, defined as declines of 10% or more, occurring on average every 2.2 years, according to data from MUFG cited by The Globe and Mail. The most recent correction came in April 2025, when the market tumbled about 20% from its peak on so-called Liberation Day. While that timing does not mean a downdraft is overdue, another correction is considered inevitable, and the S&P 500 is currently at one of its most overvalued levels on record.

The bond market is amplifying the caution. The 10-year and 20-year Treasury yields are both near their highest levels since 2002, a period that preceded the 2007–2009 Great Recession and the tail end of the bear market that followed the burst of the dot-com bubble, according to Yahoo Finance. Rising yields indicate a bond sell-off as investors demand higher compensation for perceived risk. Meanwhile, the S&P 500 is trading near all-time highs, with valuations last seen just before the dot-com bubble burst. JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon has described the risks as "tectonic plates," warning that a collision could cause a market earthquake, citing geopolitical conflict, high inflation, elevated leverage, and high stock valuations. The Federal Reserve has also begun limiting the guidance it provides, leaving bond investors without a roadmap for the first time in years, while the Fed continues to fight inflation with likely further rate hikes that could trigger a recession.

A USA Today report notes that most Americans believe a stock market correction is coming, reflecting widespread unease. Barron's has highlighted a "scary stock market divided" that has opened up, though the source material does not provide further specifics on that division.

In response to the heightened risk, some analysts recommend preparing portfolios with defensive, dividend-paying stocks that have historically weathered downturns. The Globe and Mail identifies three such stocks: Realty Income, Procter & Gamble, and WM. Realty Income, a real estate investment trust, has outperformed the S&P 500 in 11 of the 13 corrections since its 1994 public listing, declining by only 2.6% on average versus the S&P 500's average drawdown of 22.6%. It has a beta of 0.5, implying half the volatility of the broader market, and offers a 6% yield supported by a globally diversified portfolio of long-term net-leased properties. Procter & Gamble has paid dividends every year since 1890 and raised its payout for 70 consecutive years, making it a Dividend King. Its portfolio of household staples generates durable cash flows — $19.6 billion last year — and the stock yields about 3%. WM, the waste management company, has a beta roughly half that of the S&P 500, reflecting the essential nature of its services regardless of economic conditions.

A longer-term perspective from TKer by Sam Ro offers a striking illustration of the stock market's asymmetric upside. After Berkshire Hathaway announced Warren Buffett's retirement, analyst Meb Faber noted that if Berkshire declined 99% on that news, it would still have outperformed the S&P 500 since 1965, when Buffett took over. The stat underscores the power of compound interest and the potential upside of long-term holding, though it relies on a single purchase of a rare winner and a 61-year holding period. The key takeaway, the report suggests, is that the market's asymmetric upside affords investors some downside cushion, but the need to sell during a big drawdown remains a real risk.

With bond yields flashing warnings, valuations stretched, and historical patterns pointing to an eventual correction, investors are weighing how to position portfolios. Whether the current risks materialize into a full downturn or remain contained, the consensus from the sources is that preparation — through dividend stocks or a long-term horizon — is prudent.

stories.headline: Rasmussen carries no-hitter into 8th as Rays take ALDS Game 1 over Yankees
body: ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — Drew Rasmussen carried a no-hitter into the eighth inning and struck out 10 as the Tampa Bay Rays blanked the New York Yankees 1-0 on Saturday night in Game 1 of the American League Division Series before a sold-out crowd of 40,542 at Tropicana Field. Rasmussen walked two and retired 15 straight batters before Austin Wells broke up the no-hit bid with a double down the right-field line with two outs in the eighth. Wells was thrown out at third base on a relay from right fielder Victor Mesa Jr. to shortstop Taylor Walls to third baseman Junior Caminero, ending the inning and the Yankees' best scoring chance.

Rasmussen became the seventh pitcher in the Modern Era to carry a no-hit bid through 7 2/3 innings in the postseason and the first since Aníbal Sánchez did so for the Nationals in Game 1 of the 2019 National League Championship Series. He racked up a career-high 23 swinging strikes, the most by a Ray in a postseason game, mixing cutters, changeups, four-seam fastballs and two-seamers. "My heart rate was at a thousand beats per minute," Rasmussen said. "I was just trying to execute one pitch at a time."

The only run came in the third inning when first baseman Jonathan Aranda hit a solo home run off Yankees starter Gerrit Cole. Aranda crushed a 2-2 changeup that Cole tried to bury low and away but left up in the zone. "Obviously it comes down to us losing the game on that pitch; that's tough," catcher Austin Wells said. "But I would throw that pitch again probably 10 more times, and I think we'd end up with a good result." Cole allowed one run on three hits and two walks with five strikeouts over five innings. "It felt like it was leverage the whole game," Yankees manager Aaron Boone said. "I thought he threw the ball really well."

The Rays' victory gave them a 1-0 lead in the best-of-five series. In Division Series with the current 2-2-1 format, teams taking a 1-0 lead at home have gone on to win 42 of 56 times (75 percent). It was Tampa Bay's first playoff victory since Game 1 of the 2021 ALDS. "If you look it up, the definition of ace, in my opinion, is Drew Rasmussen," Aranda said. "He's done it for us the entire year."

Rasmussen, whom pitching coach Kyle Snyder called "the industry standard" and "the most underrated starting pitcher in baseball for the last five years," improved to 5-2 with a 1.81 ERA in 11 career regular-season games (10 starts) against the Yankees. Manager Kevin Cash had compared Rasmussen's work ethic to Hall of Famer Roy Halladay before his final regular-season start, when Rasmussen carried a no-hitter into the seventh inning against New York. "I've said a lot of dumb things in my life," Cash said. "That one was not."

Wells, who was thrown out trying to stretch his double into a triple, said he was "trying to make something happen" for an offense that had been held hitless until his hit. Boone called it "obviously not a good decision there." Mesa, who has one of the stronger outfield arms in the sport, said he knew Wells "is not that fast" and focused on getting the ball in. "I could just feel Wells put his head down and commit to going to third when he was maybe 10-15 feet before he hit second," Walls said. "I just knew that I had a lot of time."

stories.headline: Congo Ebola outbreak: clinical trial tests experimental pill to prevent infection
stories.byline: Health & Science desk · anchored on AP
body: More than 250 participants have been enrolled in a clinical trial in eastern Congo testing an experimental antiviral pill designed to prevent Ebola infection after exposure, as the country battles its deadliest outbreak of the disease. The trial, which began in July, is testing Gilead’s obeldesivir, given within five days of suspected contact with the virus to stop the disease from developing — an approach known as post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP). The drug targets the Bundibugyo virus, the strain responsible for the current outbreak, for which no approved vaccine or treatment exists.

At least 8,300 confirmed cases, including 4,000 deaths, have been recorded since the outbreak was declared in mid-May in eastern Congo. It has spread to seven provinces and continues to outpace efforts to track and slow it, according to authorities. The trial, coordinated by the medical nonprofit ALIMA, aims to recruit nearly 1,000 adults and children over age 12 who have had contact with a confirmed case within the past five days but show no symptoms. Half will receive a placebo. Participants are monitored daily for 21 days, with a final follow-up call after 42 days, said Dr. Godefroid Basara, who is working on the trial.

One participant who enrolled in August after her husband tested positive for Ebola told the Associated Press that so far no one in her family has developed symptoms. 'I realized that if I even touched my husband — and I did touch him, his vomit, everything — (it meant that) I was a direct contact. I could have also passed on this contagious disease. I could have been contaminated,' she said. Another participant said two family members had caught Ebola and one had died. 'This disease is killing. It's better to take precautions,' he said. Both participants requested anonymity to protect their privacy.

ALIMA said that if trial participants begin to develop symptoms, they will immediately receive supportive treatment, which has been shown to be helpful when symptoms are caught early. 'It differs from a vaccine, which may take days or weeks to provide protection. It is also different from curative treatment because it is intended for people who are not yet showing symptoms,' said ALIMA research coordinator Dr. Guilavogui Jean Paul Yassa. If the pill proves effective, it could help break the chain of infection.

Dr. Jacques Zawadi, an investigating physician at the trial center, said most participants are happy to take part, but the study has faced challenges encouraging people who live far from the center to sign up. He noted that the study is sometimes disrupted when participants learn that family members have died from the disease. 'This is the biggest challenge we face. When a person is emotionally affected, it is not easy to reason with them and ensure they return to the study,' he said. Trial partners also include Congo’s National Institute of Biomedical Research and the French institute ANRS Emerging Infectious Diseases.

Separately, Congo has begun vaccinating health workers with the Ervebo vaccine, which was effective against a different, more common Ebola virus during previous outbreaks. Authorities have said Ervebo could offer some protection against Bundibugyo, but whether it can prevent illness is still being studied. The World Health Organization has said the outbreak continues to outpace efforts to track and slow its spread and is on track to exceed the 2014–2016 West Africa outbreak, the deadliest on record, which killed 11,000 people. On Thursday, Doctors Without Borders said a staff member had tested positive for Ebola and was being evacuated to the Netherlands.

stories.headline: OpenAI safety employee resigns, warns of broken culture
body: David Robinson, a safety employee at OpenAI who led the writing of safety reports accompanying major product launches, has resigned and is publicly warning that the company's culture is 'broken.' In an essay published in The Atlantic, Robinson, who said he is 'among the longest-tenured employees at the company' with three-and-a-half years at OpenAI, argued that the broader Silicon Valley culture of 'extreme confidence' and 'perpetual sprints' has led AI companies to build bigger models with 'unimpeded optimism' while underestimating potential problems.

Robinson wrote that OpenAI's approach of 'iterative deployment' — looking for problems and improving guardrails in response — 'by its very nature, guarantees periodic failures — and the scale of those failures is growing as systems get more capable.' He pointed to a recent breach of Hugging Face systems by OpenAI agents and continuing revelations of OpenAI discovering more rogue agents as evidence. 'An environment where things like this can happen is no place to grow artificial minds that could be smarter than we are and that might not do what we want them to,' he wrote.

Given today's risks, Robinson argued that frontier AI companies need to operate 'like nuclear-power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster.' He said that during his time at OpenAI, he 'never encountered a colleague who had experience making airplanes fly safely or nuclear reactors run without melting down, or helping the financial system grow without collapsing.' Robinson also called for bigger questions about alignment, saying current 'measures of how well' AI systems 'match human values are coarse.' 'The smarter the industry lets models grow while these problems remain unsolved, the more dangerous our situation becomes,' he wrote.

In response to Robinson's essay, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company continues to improve its safety measures. 'We're making sure our models don't become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down,' Pusateri said in a statement. 'We're making significant changes to strengthen security in our research and testing environments, train models to not just complete tasks but do so responsibly, expand our work with third-party evaluators, and improve real-time monitoring so we can detect and respond to concerning behavior earlier in the training process.'

Robinson is the latest in a growing number of researchers and safety workers who have left prominent AI firms. Jacob Coxon, who worked at both OpenAI and Anthropic, quit and declared that these companies are 'gambling with our lives.' He was followed by Robert O'Callahan, Bilal Chughtai, and Josh Engels at Google DeepMind, as well as Joe Benton at Anthropic. Coxon's comments led to a broader debate about AI safety, with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei unveiling a plan for more cautious AI development, and AI executives meeting with President Donald Trump this week to sign a non-binding pledge to implement more safety controls.

Robinson acknowledged that he is following a common step in the AI whistleblower playbook by hiring a PR firm, but insisted, 'The decision to speak out is mine alone.' He said he concluded that 'stronger incentives for safety — coming from outside the company — are a big part of getting this right.' 'Perhaps I should have stayed and fought for fundamental shifts in our staffing and culture, but in practice, my colleagues and I were so busy sprinting that we seldom had the chance to consider big changes, much less to actually make them,' he wrote.

stories.headline: Trump names Jay Clayton to lead new federal AI task force
body: President Donald Trump on Sunday named Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to lead a new White House task force on artificial intelligence, giving the group 120 days to research and report on the technology's risks and opportunities and to recommend how the federal government should respond.

Trump is calling the group the "Super Intelligence Force," or SI, because he prefers the term "super intelligence" over AI. In a Truth Social post Sunday, Trump said the task force "will coordinate the Federal Government's engagement with Consumers, Public Interest Groups, Religious Organizations, Critical Infrastructure Providers, and Super Intelligence Companies." The task force will report to Trump and his chief of staff, Susie Wiles.

In addition to Clayton, the task force includes Federal Trade Commission Chairman Andrew Ferguson; Emil Michael, the Defense Department's under secretary of war for research and engineering and chief technology officer; and Scott Kupor, director of the Office of Personnel Management. The Wall Street Journal first reported Clayton's new role Saturday.

Clayton, a former chair of the Securities and Exchange Commission and U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York, was confirmed by the Senate as DNI in July, giving him authority over 18 U.S. intelligence agencies. The announcement comes days after AI industry leaders met with Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson at the White House and signed onto a voluntary safety agreement that Trump called "morally binding."

Trump has so far opposed regulation of AI, despite calls from industry leaders such as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman for federal guardrails on frontier AI models. In a September Truth Social post, Trump said he would create a new "AI Force" to help the industry and root out bad actors, adding, "We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry. Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows!" He also suggested AI fears were a hoax and blamed "Radical Left Dumocrats."

Venture capitalist David Sacks had previously served as AI and crypto czar under Trump, but in March said his time as a special government employee had ended. Sacks remains co-chair of the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, a federal advisory committee of outside experts on technology, scientific research and innovation.
